entries.title: A test is a measurable rejection probability
entries.summary: A randomized test assigns each observation a rejection probability between zero and one.
entries.statement:
φ : Ω → [0, 1] is measurable.

Our encoding uses nonnegative extended real values bounded by 1. This excludes infinity and retains the measurable-space formulation.
assumptions: Ω is a measurable space.
The formal test representation is ℝ≥0∞-valued and bounded by one.
entries.notes: Encoded foundation. Equivalence of this test type with the real interval-valued test type remains to be formalized.

entries.title: The hypothesis-testing trade-off
entries.summary: For a type-I error budget α, minimize the achievable type-II error.
entries.statement:
T(P, Q)(α) = inf { E_Q[1 − φ] : E_P[φ] ≤ α, φ measurable, 0 ≤ φ ≤ 1 }.

The first distribution controls type-I error; the second controls type-II error. The Lean definition uses a complete-lattice infimum and nonnegative integrals.
assumptions: P and Q are probability measures on the same measurable space.
α belongs to [0,1].
entries.notes: The real-test, error, feasibility and infimum correspondence is proved by tradeOff_eq_real_test_infimum. Independent source-fidelity review remains outstanding.

entries.title: The zero test has zero type-I error
entries.summary: Never rejecting the null hypothesis gives no false rejection.
entries.statement: typeIError P zeroTest = 0.
assumptions: P is a probability measure.
entries.notes: Auxiliary lemma for the encoded testing problem; not a numbered main theorem of the paper.

entries.title: The zero test has unit type-II error
entries.summary: A test that never rejects always accepts under the alternative.
entries.statement: typeIIError Q zeroTest = 1.
assumptions: Q is a probability measure.
entries.notes: The normalization Q(Ω)=1 supplies the unit value.

entries.title: More type-I budget lowers the trade-off
entries.summary: Increasing α enlarges the admissible set of tests, so its infimum cannot increase.
entries.statement: If α ≤ β, then T(P,Q)(β) ≤ T(P,Q)(α).
assumptions: P and Q are probability measures.
α, β belong to [0,1].
entries.notes: No existence of an optimal test is assumed.

entries.title: The trade-off is at most one
entries.summary: The zero test is feasible for every significance level and has type-II error one.
entries.statement:
T(P,Q)(α) ≤ 1.

Nonnegativity is built into the encoded codomain, so this also excludes infinite trade-off values.
assumptions: P and Q are probability measures.
α belongs to [0,1].
entries.notes: This is weaker than the complete trade-off-function characterization.

entries.title: Removal and preservation together
entries.summary: The edited distribution should be distinguishable from the unwanted population while remaining close to the retained population.
entries.statement:
T(p, p₁) ≤ f_d  and  f_c ≤ T(p, q₁).

The order is pointwise in the significance level. The encoded predicate accepts arbitrary baseline curves; the paper restricts them to realizable trade-off functions.
assumptions: p, p₁, q₁ are probability measures on a common measurable space.
Baseline admissibility and family membership are additional source-facing restrictions, not encoded here.
entries.notes: Generalized baseline predicate. No Gaussian baseline formula, Blackwell converse, or statistical algorithm is assumed.

entries.title: Weaker requirements preserve unlearning
entries.summary: Increase the allowed removal curve and decrease the required preservation curve; an already feasible distribution stays feasible.
entries.statement: If p satisfies (f_d, f_c) unlearning, f_d ≤ f′_d and f′_c ≤ f_c, then p satisfies (f′_d, f′_c) unlearning.
assumptions: The original pair of inequalities holds.
The removal requirement is weakened pointwise.
The preservation requirement is weakened pointwise.
entries.notes: Proved for the generalized encoded predicate. The argument uses only order transitivity.

entries.title: The feasible edited distributions
entries.summary: Restrict the two unlearning inequalities to the chosen distribution family.
entries.statement:
ℛ = { p ∈ 𝒫 : T(p,p₁) ≤ f_d and f_c ≤ T(p,q₁) }.

The paper also places the reference distributions in 𝒫 and requires realizable baselines. Those source restrictions must be supplied separately to this generalized predicate.
assumptions: 𝒫 is a set of probability measures on Ω.
entries.notes: A definition is not a characterization theorem for any particular population family.

entries.title: Unfolding membership in the feasible region
entries.summary: Membership means belonging to the family and satisfying both pointwise bounds.
entries.statement: p ∈ ℛ ↔ p ∈ 𝒫 ∧ T(p,p₁) ≤ f_d ∧ f_c ≤ T(p,q₁).
assumptions: Only the typing data of the defined feasible region.
entries.notes: Definitional unfolding, explicitly distinguished from a statistical result.

entries.title: Weaker requirements enlarge the feasible region
entries.summary: The consistency observation lifts to inclusion of feasible sets.
entries.statement: f_d ≤ f′_d and f′_c ≤ f_c imply ℛ(f_d,f_c) ⊆ ℛ(f′_d,f′_c).
assumptions: The same family and reference distributions are used.
Both baseline inequalities hold pointwise.
entries.notes: An auxiliary consequence of the encoded definitions.

entries.title: The metric feasible set
entries.summary: R(u,v;a,e) = { x : a ≤ dist(x,u) and dist(x,v) ≤ e }.
entries.statement: R(u,v;a,e) = { x : a ≤ dist(x,u) and dist(x,v) ≤ e }.
assumptions: X is a pseudometric space.
The two radii are real numbers; no sign assumption is needed to define the set.
entries.notes: A geometric prerequisite for Gaussian results. The Gaussian testing-to-distance bridge is not yet proved.

entries.title: Unfolding the geometric constraints
entries.summary: x ∈ R(u,v;a,e) ↔ a ≤ dist(x,u) ∧ dist(x,v) ≤ e.
entries.statement: x ∈ R(u,v;a,e) ↔ a ≤ dist(x,u) ∧ dist(x,v) ≤ e.
assumptions: X is a pseudometric space.
No sign assumptions on the real thresholds.
entries.notes: Definitional unfolding; no Gaussian result is claimed.

entries.title: Feasibility implies preservation
entries.summary: R(u,v;a,e) ⊆ closedBall(v,e).
entries.statement: R(u,v;a,e) ⊆ closedBall(v,e).
assumptions: X is a pseudometric space.
No sign assumptions on the real thresholds.
entries.notes: A direct consequence of the second metric inequality.

entries.title: A feasible point bounds the removal radius
entries.summary: x ∈ R(u,v;a,e) implies a ≤ dist(u,v) + e.
entries.statement: x ∈ R(u,v;a,e) implies a ≤ dist(u,v) + e.
assumptions: X is a pseudometric space.
The pointwise bound additionally assumes x is feasible.
entries.notes: An individual-point version of the necessary nonemptiness bound.

entries.title: Zero removal leaves the preservation ball
entries.summary: R(u,v;0,e) = closedBall(v,e).
entries.statement: R(u,v;0,e) = closedBall(v,e).
assumptions: X is a pseudometric space.
No nonnegativity premise on e is needed; for negative e both sets are empty.
entries.notes: This checks the geometric boundary case flagged in the source review. It does not establish the Gaussian trade-off formula.

entries.title: Nonemptiness bounds the removal radius
entries.summary: R(u,v;a,e) ≠ ∅ implies a ≤ dist(u,v) + e.
entries.statement: R(u,v;a,e) ≠ ∅ implies a ≤ dist(u,v) + e.
assumptions: X is a pseudometric space.
The geometric feasible set is nonempty.
entries.notes: The necessary geometric direction uses only the triangle inequality. The converse needs extra geometry.

entries.title: Separation makes the whole ball feasible
entries.summary: a + e ≤ dist(u,v) implies R(u,v;a,e) = closedBall(v,e).
entries.statement: a + e ≤ dist(u,v) implies R(u,v;a,e) = closedBall(v,e).
assumptions: X is a pseudometric space.
The displayed separation inequality holds.
entries.notes: A sufficient condition only. Necessity is not claimed, including at zero removal radius.

entries.title: Real and encoded testing trade-offs agree
entries.summary: The encoded curve equals the infimum of real type-II expectations over the paper's feasible measurable tests.
entries.statement: For probability measures P,Q and α in [0,1], the real value of the encoded trade-off equals the infimum over measurable real tests φ in [0,1] satisfying E_P[φ] ≤ α, of E_Q[1−φ].
assumptions: P and Q are probability measures on the same measurable space.
α is represented by a finite ENNReal value in [0,1].
entries.notes: This proves Definition 1's representation bridge; independent source-fidelity review and the realizable-baseline interface remain open.

entries.title: Blackwell ordering and data processing
entries.summary: Relate testing order to Markov-kernel comparison, with the measurable-space hypotheses audited explicitly.
entries.statement: The kernel-to-order direction is proved for the real-test infimum. The converse, including its measurable-space hypotheses, remains open.
assumptions: Exact regularity assumptions remain under source review.
entries.notes: The full equivalence remains unproved. The checked forward direction is tracked separately; independent source review is outstanding.

entries.title: The Gaussian feasible region
entries.summary: Identify simultaneous removal and preservation constraints through Gaussian testing and Mahalanobis geometry.
entries.statement: Separate Gaussian testing from geometry, then handle zero removal threshold, coincident centers and general covariance explicitly.
assumptions: Nondegenerate covariance and parameter domains must be stated precisely.
entries.notes: Source audit found a zero-threshold boundary issue and a metric ambiguity. See the audit notes before formalizing this target.

entries.title: Composition across independent domains
entries.summary: Compose removal and preservation trade-offs over product distributions.
entries.statement: Develop product measures and testing comparisons, prove tensor composition is well defined, and derive the unlearning inequalities.
assumptions: Independent product structure; further hypotheses depend on the chosen comparison theorem.
entries.notes: No composition theorem is admitted as an axiom.

entries.title: Beyond finite-dimensional Gaussians
entries.summary: Gaussian white noise, log-concave location models, Poisson and multiple populations need separate developments.
entries.statement: Track support and identifiability, generalized inverse conventions, unions of excluded intervals, and nontrivial Cameron–Martin spaces.
assumptions: Family-specific hypotheses are not yet finalized.
entries.notes: Several printed claims require correction or additional conditions; no family-level theorem is currently certified.

entries.title: Finite-sample removal algorithms
entries.summary: Formalize the sampling algorithms and probability bounds underlying random and selective removal.
entries.statement: Encode independent samples, positive edited sample sizes, concentration and confidence allocation. Check every finite-sample constant.
assumptions: Sampling independence, sample-size restrictions and confidence domains must be explicit.
entries.notes: The random-removal confidence-bookkeeping issue does not itself disprove its final bound; the review outlines a direct pooled-Gaussian repair.

entries.title: Ordering generalized inverses
entries.summary: Pointwise ordering of two functions preserves ordering of their generalized left inverses.
entries.statement: If f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x ∈ [0,1], then f⁻¹(t) ≤ g⁻¹(t). The inverse is the infimum of the sublevel set in [0,1], with empty infimum defined as 1.
assumptions: f and g map the closed unit interval to itself and are nonincreasing, as in the source.
Pointwise ordering f(x) ≤ g(x) on [0,1].
The threshold t belongs to [0,1].
entries.notes: The subtype bridge identifies the paper’s [0,1]-valued sublevel infimum with the real extension, including the empty-set value 1. A separate independent assistant pass reviewed the source-shaped statement; human review remains welcome.

entries.title: Kernel post-processing raises the testing trade-off
entries.summary: If both laws pass through the same Markov kernel, the real-valued testing trade-off cannot decrease.
entries.statement: T(P,Q)(α) ≤ T(KP,KQ)(α), with both sides given by infima over measurable real tests as in Definition 1.
assumptions: P,Q are probability measures on a common measurable space.
K is a Markov kernel to the target measurable space.
α is represented in [0,1].
entries.notes: This is only the kernel-to-order direction of Theorem 19. Its converse and independent source-fidelity review remain open.
